one_liner: LLVM-based ahead-of-time WebAssembly runtime in C++; fastest total in the 2021 libsodium shootout against Wasmtime, Wasmer and V8.
what_it_does: WAVM is a non-browser WebAssembly VM that parses binary or text modules, validates them and compiles each whole module to native code with LLVM before running it. It supports WebAssembly 1.0 plus SIMD, threads, reference types, multi-value, bulk memory, exception handling, multi-memory and memory64, and ships a WASI implementation. Embedders use its own C++ Runtime API (Compartment, Context, compileModule / loadPrecompiledModule, instantiateModule, invokeFunction) or the WebAssembly C API binding in wavm-c.h; the `wavm` CLI runs, compiles, assembles and disassembles modules.
how_it_is_fast: Each module is translated to LLVM IR and run through LLVM's default O2 module pipeline for the host target machine, so code is optimized up front and tuned to the running CPU instead of being tiered up from a baseline compiler. Every 32-bit linear memory reserves 8 GB of virtual address space plus guard pages, so a 32-bit index plus 32-bit offset can never leave the reservation and bounds checks are elided; out-of-bounds accesses fault on a guard page and signal handlers turn the fault into a WebAssembly trap. The price is compile time, which can be cached (`wavm compile` precompiled objects, WAVM_OBJECT_CACHE_DIR with LMDB).
when_to_use: Long-running, compute-heavy guest code (crypto, codecs, number crunching) where peak throughput on plain WebAssembly matters and LLVM compile time is amortized.
Hosts that can precompile or cache object code (`wavm compile`, object cache) so restarts do not pay the LLVM compile again, e.g. serverless designs like FAASM that the benchmark author points to.
C++ embedders that need many post-MVP proposals in one engine: SIMD, threads, exception handling, multi-memory, memory64 and WASI.
64-bit x86-64 or AArch64 hosts on Windows, macOS or Linux with 4 KB pages (all six combinations are in CI).
when_not_to_use: Startup- or latency-sensitive work and many short-lived modules: the whole module goes through LLVM O2 before the first instruction runs; the EOS VM README calls WAVM's compile times 'extremely long and unpredictable', and the benchmark numbers exclude compile time.
Running untrusted code next to sensitive data: the README says WAVM is vulnerable to some side-channel attacks such as Spectre variant 2 and recommends OS-process isolation.
32-bit hosts or address-space-limited environments (ulimit -v, many instances): the runtime needs a 64-bit host and reserves 8 GB plus guard pages per 32-bit memory.
AArch64 Linux with 64 KB kernel pages: issue #391 (2026-08, NVIDIA GH200) reports a SEGV during runtime creation, with no maintainer reply.

Teams that need versioned releases or a deep maintainer bench: one maintainer, only nightly tags, a four-year gap from 2022-05 to 2026-04, and a hard dependency on LLVM 20+ (a patched WAVM-LLVM 21 is recommended, especially on macOS).

integration.dependencies: LLVM 20+ (WAVM-LLVM 21 recommended); vendored BLAKE2, liblmdb (object cache) and libunwind
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.16, LLVM 20; GCC or Clang on Linux, Xcode on macOS, Visual Studio 2022 on Windows
integration.platforms: x86-64 and AArch64 on Windows, macOS and Linux (CI-tested); 64-bit hosts only; x86 target CPU must support SSE 4.1; prebuilt macOS binaries are arm64 only
integration.thread_safety: not documented in Runtime.h; the API separates Compartment (object ownership, garbage collection) from Context (execution state, createContext/cloneContext), and the WebAssembly threads proposal (shared memory, atomics) is supported
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — offers a WebAssembly C API binding (wavm-c.h) and a `wavm run` CLI with WASI, but its native C++ API (compartments, GC roots, contexts) is WAVM-specific and it has no Rust API like Wasmtime or Wasmer

gotchas: Each 32-bit linear memory reserves 8 GB of virtual address space plus guard bytes, so thousands of instances can exhaust address space or hit overcommit and ulimit -v limits (issue #245 asks why WebAssembly VMs take so much memory).
Traps arrive through signal handlers on guard-page faults; wrap calls in catchRuntimeExceptions / unwindSignalsAsExceptions and check how they interact with the host's own SIGSEGV handlers.

Runtime objects are garbage-collected per Compartment and must be held through GCPointer roots; raw pointers die at collectCompartmentGarbage, and bug #74 (open since 2018) says the GC does not scan functions on the stack.

The benchmark totals are dominated by a few memory-hard tests: on WAVM's macOS logs pwhash_scrypt is 23.9% of the summed time and the top four tests 68%, and pwhash_scrypt alone accounts for 84% of WAVM's total-time lead over wasmer-llvm (my count from the per-test logs).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick WAVM over Wasmtime, Wasmer or WasmEdge when peak throughput on plain WebAssembly matters more than compile latency and you want an LLVM AOT engine with broad proposal support inside a C++ host; aWsm (13.4% vs WAVM's 28.1% slowdown over native in its paper) and wasm2c or w2c2 can run faster but need an offline C or LLVM compile step, and interpreters (WAMR, wasm3, Fizzy) start far faster but run code tens of times slower.
verified_claims_summary: In Frank Denis's 2021-Q1 libsodium 1.0.18 WASI benchmark (LLVM 11.1.0 plus wasm-opt -O4, all runtimes built from git on 2021-02-21, unnamed Intel macOS laptop, each test timing 128 iterations inside the guest with CLOCK_MONOTONIC, compile and initialization excluded, one logged value per test), WAVM had the lowest summed time: 4.63 vs Node/V8 5.23, wasmer-llvm 5.44, wasmtime 6.65 and lucet 11.61 (native 2.04). My recount of the 59 per-test logs gives geomean time ratios to WAVM of wasmtime 1.47x, node 1.20x and wasmer-llvm 1.09x, with wasmer-llvm faster on 16 tests, node on 2 and wasmtime on 1 (auth3), so the page's 'every single test' and 'about 15% faster than wasmer' overstate a per-test margin of about 9%; the 2026 rerun (search snippet only) puts Wasmer first with WAVM close.
status_note: Active again after a 2022-05 to 2026-04 gap: an LLVM 21 and C++17 overhaul plus fixes on 2026-04-02/04, nightly-only releases (VERSION 0.0.0-prerelease) and a single maintainer; BSD-3-Clause and copyable, but heavy to vendor because it needs LLVM 20+.
